Option A: The number is always positive when
the qualifier 'unsigned' is used. This is correct.
When a variable is declared as 'unsigned', it
means that it can only represent non-negative
values, including zero. This is because the sign bit
is not reserved, and all bits in the variable's
memory representation are used to represent the
magnitude of the value. So, unsigned variables
can only hold positive values or zero.
Option B: The number can be positive or
negative when the qualifier 'signed' is used.
This is correct. When a variable is declared as
'signed', it means that it can represent both
positive and negative values. The variable
reserves one bit for the sign, usually the leftmost
bit (the most significant bit). If this bit is 0, the
number is positive, and if it's 1, the number is
negative. The rest of the bits represent the
magnitude of the value.
Option C: The range of values for signed data
types is more than that of unsigned data types.
This statement is incorrect. The range of values
for signed data types is typically less than that of
unsigned data types. For example, an 8-bit

to 255, whereas an 8-bit signed data type can

may cause starvation:
This statement is true. SRTF scheduling prioritizes
the process with the shortest remaining
execution time, which can lead to longer
processes being repeatedly preempted by
shorter ones. If there are always shorter
processes arriving, longer processes may never
get a chance to execute, leading to starvation.
2. Preemptive scheduling may cause starvation:
This statement is true. Preemptive scheduling
allows the operating system to interrupt the
execution of a process to give access to the CPU
to another process. If there are processes with
higher priority constantly arriving, lower priority
processes may be repeatedly preempted and
may never get a chance to execute, resulting in
starvation.
3. Round robin is better than FCFS in terms of
response time:
This statement is true. Round-robin scheduling
ensures fairness by providing each process with a
fixed time slice to execute before being
preempted, which helps in achieving better
response time compared to first-come, first-
served (FCFS) scheduling, especially when there
are long-running processes.
So option D is the correct answer.

Silly Window Syndrome is a problem that arises
due to poor implementation of TCP. It degrades
the TCP performance and makes the data
transmission extremely inefficient. The problem is
called so because:
It causes the sender window size to shrink to
a silly value.
The window size shrinks to such an extent
that the data being transmitted is smaller than
TCP Header.
The two major causes of this syndrome are as
follows:
The sender window transmits one byte of data
repeatedly.
The receiver window accepts one byte of data
repeatedly.
Cause-1: Sender window transmitting one
byte of data repeatedly –
Suppose only one byte of data is generated
by an application. The poor implementation of
TCP leads to the transmission of this small
segment of data. Every time the application
generates a byte of data, the window
transmits it. This makes the transmission
process slow and inefficient. The problem is
solved by Nagle’s algorithm.
Nagle’s algorithm suggests:
The sender should send only the first byte on
receiving one-byte data from the application.
The sender should buffer all the rest bytes
until the outstanding byte gets
acknowledged.
The sender should wait for 1 RTT(Round Trip
Time).
After receiving the acknowledgment, the
sender should send the buffered data in one
TCP segment. Then, the sender should buffer
the data again until the previously sent data
gets acknowledged.
Cause-2: Receiver window accepting one byte
of data repeatedly –
Suppose consider the case when the receiver
is unable to process all the incoming data. In
such a case, the receiver will advertise a small
window size. The process continues and the
window size becomes smaller and smaller. A
stage arrives when it repeatedly advertises a
window size of 1 byte. This makes the
receiving process slow and inefficient. The
solution to this problem is Clark’s Solution.
Clark’s solution suggests:
The receiver should not send a window
update for 1 byte.
The receiver should wait until it has a decent
amount of space available.
The receiver should then advertise that
window size to the sender.
So option A is the correct answer.

explanation.value:
The Classification algorithm is a Supervised
Learning technique that is used to identify the
category of new observations on the basis of
training data. In Classification, a program learns
from the given dataset or observations and then
classifies new observations into a number of
classes or groups.
I. Logistic regression: Logistic regression is a
classification algorithm used to model the
probability of a binary outcome based on one or
more predictor variables. It is commonly used for
binary classification tasks, where the outcome
variable is categorical and has two possible
classes.
II. Backpropagation is a learning algorithm used
in artificial neural networks for training
feedforward neural networks. It is typically used
for supervised learning tasks, including both
regression and classification.
III. Linear regression: Linear regression is a
regression algorithm used to model the
relationship between a dependent variable and
one or more independent variables. It is used for
predicting continuous numeric outcomes rather
than categorical classes. Therefore, it is not a
classification algorithm.
IV. Forward propagation: Forward propagation is
a step in the process of training a feedforward
neural network. It involves passing the input data
forward through the network's layers to produce
an output.
So option C is the correct answer.

Which Boolean operation on two variables can be represented by a single perceptron layer?
I. X1 AND X2
II. X1 OR X2
III. X1 NOR X2
IV. X1 XOR X2

explanation.value:
Linearly separable boolean functions can be
solved using a perceptron. If you can draw a line
to divide inputs of distinct classes,  then the
problem is linearly separable.
It can be represented as AND, OR, and NOR as
follows:
- AND Operation: Mapping allows linear solutions
for each set of inputs (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1). Two
classes—one for outputs that should be 0 and
another for outputs that should be 1 which can
be created from the points.
- OR Operation: The OR operation is linearly
separable, much like the AND operation. It is
possible to distinguish between the (1,0),(0,1),
and (1,1) inputs that yield 0 and those that yield 1.
- NOR Operation: The NOR operation is linearly
separable, just like the OR operation. To put it
simply, the NOR operation is the opposite of the
OR operation.
But the XOR operation is not linearly separable;
that is, the data for 0 and 1 cannot be separated
by a straight line. Consequently, a single-layer
perceptron cannot represent it.
So option C is the correct answer.

Select the correct order of events after power is
initialized on a system.
I. Bootstrap loader is loaded from the disk
II. Kernel is loaded onto the memory
III. Firmware ROM loads boot block

explanation.value:
Firmware ROM loads boot block (III): When you
turn the power on in a computing system, a built-
in piece of software called firmware, which is
stored in ROM (Read-Only Memory), is activated
first. This firmware includes a program called
BIOS (Basic Input/Output System). These
programs start the boot process by performing a
power-on self-test (POST) to check the health of
the system’s hardware. Then, they look for a
bootable device (like a hard disk, USB drive, etc.).
From this device, it loads the boot block, also
known as the Master Boot Record (MBR) or GUID
Partition Table (GPT) in UEFI systems. This boot
block contains information about the layout of
the storage device and points to the location of
the bootloader.
Bootstrap loader is loaded from the disk (I): The
boot block points to the location of the
bootloader in secondary storage (hard disk, SSD,
USB, etc.). The firmware loads this bootloader,
known as a bootstrap loader, into memory. The
job of the bootloader is to load and initiate the
operating system.
Kernel is loaded onto the memory (II): Once the
bootloader is in memory, it loads the operating
system kernel into memory. The kernel is the core
component of an operating system and interacts
directly with the system’s hardware. When the
kernel is ready, it starts the operating system –
bringing us to a state where the system is ready
to run applications.
So option B is the correct answer.
